hints: Think about how many reactant molecules go in and how many product molecules come out when something adds across a C=C double bond.
walkthrough:
Picture what addition means**
Think of the C=C double bond in propene. In addition, nothing is lost or split off. Two separate small molecules, here $\text{CO}$ and $\text{H}_2$, both join onto the alkene framework to give a bigger single molecule.
Final answer: A reaction in which two or more reactants combine to form only one single product.

hints: Compare structures A and B in Fig. 3.1. They have the same carbon skeleton and same CHO group, but check where the CHO group is attached.
walkthrough:
Check what is the same and what moves**
Both A, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, and B, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCHO}$, have molecular formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}$ and both contain the aldehyde functional group. The only difference is the position of the $\text{CHO}$ group on the carbon chain, straight chain versus branched. That is positional isomerism.
Final answer: Positional isomerism.

hints: Count the longest chain including the aldehyde carbon in A, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, and remember aldehydes end in -al.
walkthrough:
Name the straight chain aldehyde**
Structure A has four carbons in a continuous chain with the $\text{CHO}$ carbon counted as C1: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$. A four carbon aldehyde is butanal, no numbers needed because the $\text{CHO}$ is always at the end.
Final answer: Butanal.

hints: Start from moles of propene used, $5.00 \times 10^3$ kg with $M_r = 42.0$, then use the 1:1 mole ratio to total aldehyde and take 96% for A with $M_r = 72.0$.
walkthrough:
Work through moles to mass**
Moles of propene = mass / $M_r$. Convert $5.00 \times 10^3$ kg to $5000$ kg and keep kg consistent: $$\text{moles propene} = 5000 / 42.0$$ Each mole of propene gives one mole of total aldehyde, so moles of A = $0.96 \times \text{moles propene}$. Then mass of A = moles $\times 72.0$: $$\text{mass A} = 0.96 \times (5000/42.0) \times 72.0 \approx 8230 \text{ kg}$$
Final answer: $96\% \times (5000/42.0) \times 72.0 = 8230$ kg (8229 kg accepted).

hints: Recall that the C=O bond is polar with C delta+ and O delta-, so think about which atom the CN- nucleophile will attack.
Remember the first step breaks the C=O pi bond onto oxygen, forming a negatively charged alkoxide intermediate.
Think about what the lone pair on the cyanide carbon does and where the second curly arrow starts and ends.
Consider how the O- intermediate picks up H+ from HCN or water to give the final cyanohydrin C.
walkthrough:
Spot the electrophile**
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the carbonyl is polarised $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$. Show that dipole clearly. The carbon is electron poor and loves nucleophiles.

Attack by cyanide**
$\text{CN}^-$ provides the nucleophile through a lone pair on carbon. Draw a curly arrow from that lone pair to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$. At the same time draw a curly arrow from the C=O double bond onto the oxygen to give $\text{O}^-$. This forms the alkoxide intermediate $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{C(H)(CN)O}^-$.

Protonate to finish**
The $\text{O}^-$ is strongly basic. It takes $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{HCN}$ (or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$). Draw a curly arrow from the lone pair on $\text{O}^-$ to the H of HCN. This gives the cyanohydrin C, $\text{H-C(OH)(CN)-C}_3\text{H}_7$, and regenerates $\text{CN}^-$.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{CN}^-$ attacks $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$; curly arrow from lone pair on C of $\text{CN}^-$ to C, and curly arrow from C=O to O. Forms $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C(O}^-\text{)(H)CN}$ intermediate. Step 2: curly arrow from $\text{O}^-$ lone pair to $\text{H}^+$ of HCN (or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CN}$.

hints: Use the orange to green colour change to identify the oxidising agent that oxidises aldehydes but is itself reduced.
Recall which mild oxidising agent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes on warming.
Think about whether aldehydes react with bromine water under normal conditions, unlike alkenes.
walkthrough:
Link orange to green to dichromate**
Orange to green is the classic reduction of $\text{Cr(VI)}$ to $\text{Cr(III)}$. So experiment 1 must use acidified potassium dichromate, $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$, which oxidises aldehyde B to a carboxylic acid.

Link silver mirror to Tollens'**
A silver mirror on warming is the positive Tollens' test for aldehydes. The reagent is Tollens' reagent, ammoniacal $\text{AgNO}_3$, which is reduced to metallic silver.

Remember aldehydes ignore bromine water**
$\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)}$ is decolourised by alkenes, not by aldehydes. B is saturated at the functional group level, so no reaction is seen and the bromine colour remains.

Final answer: Experiment 1 reagent: acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$. Experiment 2 reagent: Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate). Experiment 3 observation: no reaction (solution stays orange / brown).

hints: Remember oxidation of an aldehyde adds one O atom to form the carboxylic acid with the same number of C and H.
walkthrough:
Add one oxygen**
Aldehyde $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}$ gains one atom of oxygen from the oxidant to become the carboxylic acid $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$. Using $[\text{O}]$ to represent the oxidising power: $$\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O} + [\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$$

hints: Look for the carbon in C attached to four different groups: H, OH, CN and the propyl chain.
walkthrough:
Find the carbon with four different attachments**
In C, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CN}$, the carbon joined to $\text{OH}$, $\text{H}$, $\text{CN}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ has four different groups. That is the chiral centre. The other carbons have at least two H atoms, so they are not chiral.
Final answer: Circle the carbon bearing OH, H, CN and $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7$: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CN}$, the first carbon on the left in Fig. 3.2.

hints: With excess H2, first think what propene becomes when H2 simply adds across the C=C bond.
Then think what happens when the aldehyde products A and B, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}$, are further reduced by H2 at the C=O bond.
walkthrough:
Form the alkane by direct hydrogenation**
Propene $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$ plus $\text{H}_2$ gives propane. Simply add two H atoms: $$\text{C}_3\text{H}_6 + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_8$$

Reduce the aldehydes to alcohols**
With excess $\text{H}_2$, the aldehydes A and B, both $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}$, gain $\text{H}_2$ across C=O to give primary alcohols. Add $\text{H}_2$: $$\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O} + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$$ The two isomeric aldehydes give two isomeric alcohols.
Final answer: Molecular formula of alkane: $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$. Molecular formula of alcohols: $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$.

hints: Recall the effect of a catalyst on the rate, and that it is not used up and does not change the yield.
Think in terms of Boltzmann distribution and how an alternative route changes the proportion of successful collisions.
walkthrough:
State the rate effect**
A cobalt catalyst speeds up the reaction, so equilibrium is reached faster, but the position of equilibrium and yield are unchanged.

Explain via activation energy**
It does this by offering a different route with lower activation energy, $E_a$. More molecules now have energy greater than $E_a$, so frequency of successful collisions increases.
Final answer: Increases the rate of reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy, $E_a$.

hints: Count moles of gas on each side of equation 1: 3 moles on the left versus 1 mole on the right.
walkthrough:
Apply Le Chatelier to pressure**
Equation 1 has $3$ moles of gas on the left, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{CO} + \text{H}_2$, and $1$ mole of gas on the right, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$. Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles to reduce pressure, so equilibrium shifts right and yield of aldehyde rises.
Final answer: Equilibrium moves to the right / to products where there are fewer moles (smaller amount) of gas.

hints: Write the expression $\Delta H_r = \Sigma \Delta H_f(\text{products}) - \Sigma \Delta H_f(\text{reactants})$ and list the three reactant values, noting $\Delta H_f(\text{H}_2)=0$.
Substitute $-187$ for product and $+52$ and $-111$ for reactants, then be careful with minus signs.
walkthrough:
Set up the formation sum**
Enthalpy of reaction = sum for products minus sum for reactants: $$\Delta H_r = \Delta H_f(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}) - [\Delta H_f(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4) + \Delta H_f(\text{CO}) + \Delta H_f(\text{H}_2)]$$ $\text{H}_2$ is an element so its $\Delta H_f = 0$.

Substitute and calculate**
$$\Delta H_r = -187 - (+52) - (-111) - 0$$ $$= -187 -52 +111 = -128 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The negative sign shows the reaction is exothermic.
Final answer: $\Delta H_r = -187 - (-111) - (+52) = -128$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

hints: Remember propanal is polar due to C=O, but all molecules also have temporary electron movements, so think which two van der Waals types must both be present.
walkthrough:
Identify both forces**
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ is a polar molecule because of the $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$ bond, so permanent dipole-permanent dipole attractions act between molecules. All molecules, polar or not, also have instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London dispersion) forces from temporary electron fluctuations.
Final answer: Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (id-id / London dispersion) AND permanent dipole-permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces.
